title: A transported control-arm check carries no information about the anchored contrast
question: Does agreement between a MAIC-transported control arm and the target's observed control arm tell an analyst whether the anchored relative effect is biased?
answer: No. The check tests prognostic transport, which an anchored contrast does not need, and cannot see effect-modification transport, which it does. A prognostic shift raised the alarm rate to 0.48 while the contrast was nearly unbiased (bias -0.03 to -0.06); a modifier shift biased the log odds ratio by 0.30 with the alarm rate at 0.044. Pooled over 18,000 analyses the check's AUROC for a biased contrast was 0.50.
findings: Prognostic shift of 0.6 SD, no modifier shift: alarm rate 0.41 to 0.48, contrast bias -0.03 to -0.06.
Modifier shift of 0.6 SD, no prognostic shift: alarm rate 0.044 to 0.050, contrast bias 0.28 to 0.30, coverage 0.78 to 0.82.
At every threshold on |z| the detection rate equaled the false-alarm rate (0.21 against 0.21 at 1.96); AUROC 0.502.
The check targets the right assumption only in unanchored comparisons, where the relative effect depends on prognostic transport; that case was not simulated.
not_answered: Binary outcome only; survival-curve and RMST versions, unanchored comparisons, offsetting prognostic mechanisms and outcome-definition or follow-up differences are not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
design: Anchored binary-outcome MAIC, individual data on A versus C and arm counts on B versus C; an unmeasured prognostic covariate and an unmeasured modifier of A's effect shifted independently between populations; 18 scenarios crossing both shifts and target size.
estimand: Anchored B-versus-A marginal log odds ratio in the target; the check's alarm as a classifier of material bias
methods_compared: transported control-arm check at several thresholds
